Google's artificial intelligence program has officially beaten a human professional Go player, marking the first time a computer has beaten a human professional in this game sans handicap.

At first I read the headline and thought, wow that's some great progress - I thought we were still some number of years away from this. Then I read this:

The IBM chess computer Deep Blue, which famously beat grandmaster Garry Kasparov in 1997, was explicitly programmed to win at the game. But AlphaGo was not preprogrammed to play Go: rather, it learned using a general-purpose algorithm that allowed it to interpret the game’s patterns, in a similar way to how a DeepMind program learned to play 49 different arcade games.

And my jaw dropped. This is huge. The game space of Go is absurdly deep with moves made early in the game potentially only having a substantial impact far later. For a general purpose algorithm to be able reach super human performance in Go, and so rapidly, is goose bumpy. I had no clue Google was getting this advanced with their DeepMind stuff. For comparison it was only a couple of years ago that they announced the program taught itself how to play dozens of different Atari games to superhuman level performance using nothing but its score and the pixels on the screen. So it had no access to the rules or what any of the images on the screen meant. It had to teach itself everything. That's a huge accomplishment but to go from that to conquering Go in a couple of years is insanely rapid progress.
